text.p: The mark is set to remain soft as Germany actively seeks to hang on to export competitiveness, high-yielders stay firm ahead of EMU and as Russian politicians slug it out in the background, financial analysts said Friday.

Most important is the convergence towards European monetary union (EMU) which makes the mark less attractive than what are now perceived to be safer -- at least safer than they were this time last year -- high-yielding instruments elsewhere.

On top of this the German administration has been actively seeking a firm dollar, and therefore a soft mark, to help German exporters and the authorities will probably not be too unhappy if it inches a little lower, analysts said.

The situation in Russia is only a minor factor for the mark although Kremlin infighting will tend to see the mark suffer on brief flurries into the dollar and Swiss franc. "We're going to see the mark continue to wilt on the Euro- crosses as people dive in a scrape what's left of the high-yield barrel," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns. "And it's really lost its sheen as far as being a long-term safe-haven trade." For example the lira has rallied from about 1150 per mark to below 1000, over 13 percent, in the past 12-months and this strong slipstream effect for European high-yielders against the hard-core countries will continue in the coming months as EMU approaches.
The mark has lost around 10 percent of its value against the dollar over the past 12-months and while downside from here is limited, it will tend to remain soft, analysts said.

The United States yields 2.25 percentage points more than Germany and the next move in U.S. rates is most likely up while in Germany it could be down. The U.S. also has a strong growth advantage and there is still a strong offical preference among the Group-of-Seven for a firm dollar.

"Any significant mark appreciation would be countered with a barrage of rhetoric and may even increase the chances of the Bundesbank easing again," said Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust.
At the recent IMF/World Bank meeting, Bunesbank president Hans Tietmeyer repeated that he favoured a strong dollar.
"I hope very much the dollar will remain strong now and in the upcoming months and years," Tietmeyer said.
A soft currency not only helps exports but is also a de facto monetary easing so will also help keep the German economy going in the face of the tight fiscal policy needed for EMU.
Even if German rates are not cut again the trough for the current cycle will be protracted as fiscal policy stays tight and inflation stays low.
The situation in Russia will continue to be only a minor irritant for the mark even though Germany is Russia's major trading partner and creditor.

"Exposure to Russia is far less significant today than it was at the beginning of the 1990s, particularly in terms of the banking sector," said Klaus Baader, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Also, compared to five years ago, Russia's relationship with the west are on a far more multilateral basis...the mark is not expected to suffer further from this factor."
